structures.name: Axillary Artery
structures.function: Main arterial supply of upper limb; continuation of subclavian artery at lateral border of first rib; gives off 6 branches in 3 parts relative to pectoralis minor
structures.location: Runs from outer border of first rib to lower border of teres major (where it becomes brachial artery); surrounded by brachial plexus cords in the axilla
structures.clinicalNotes: Axillary artery injury in anterior shoulder dislocation or proximal humerus fracture. Axillary artery aneurysm post-crutch use (crutch palsy). Cannulation for IABP if femoral access unavailable. Posterior circumflex humeral artery at risk in surgical neck fractures.

structures.name: Brachial Artery
structures.function: Main artery of the arm; palpable in antecubital fossa for blood pressure auscultation; divides into radial and ulnar arteries at neck of radius
structures.location: Runs in medial bicipital groove of arm, medial to biceps brachii; superficial in antecubital fossa medial to biceps tendon; lies on brachialis muscle
structures.clinicalNotes: Volkmann's ischaemic contracture: supracondylar fracture of humerus in children compresses brachial artery → forearm compartment syndrome → flexion contracture. Site for arterial blood gas sampling and NIBP auscultation. Brachial artery injury in cardiac catheterisation via radial approach is avoided.

structures.name: Median Nerve
structures.function: Motor to LOAF muscles of hand (Lumbricals 1&2, Opponens pollicis, Abductor pollicis brevis, Flexor pollicis brevis); sensory to lateral 3.5 digits; palmar branch sensory to thenar eminence
structures.location: Formed from medial and lateral cords of brachial plexus (C6-T1); descends with brachial artery; enters forearm between heads of pronator teres; passes through carpal tunnel
structures.bloodSupply: Vasa nervorum from brachial and anterior interosseous arteries
structures.clinicalNotes: Carpal tunnel syndrome: compression at wrist → thenar wasting, loss of pinch. Ape hand deformity. Pronator teres syndrome: compression in forearm. Anterior interosseous nerve palsy: loss of OK sign (flexor pollicis longus + FDP index). Test: thumb-index pinch = O shape.

structures.name: Ulnar Nerve
structures.function: Motor to intrinsic muscles (interossei, hypothenar, adductor pollicis, medial 2 lumbricals); sensory to medial 1.5 digits; 'the nerve of fine movement'
structures.location: From medial cord C8-T1; descends posteromedial to brachial artery; passes posterior to medial epicondyle (cubital tunnel); runs with ulnar artery in forearm; passes through Guyon's canal at wrist
structures.clinicalNotes: Cubital tunnel syndrome: most common site at medial epicondyle — clawing of ring+little finger, weakness of grip, wasting of hypothenar and interossei. Wartenberg sign: little finger abduction. Froment sign: adductor pollicis weakness. Guyon canal compression from cyclists.

structures.name: Radial Nerve
structures.function: Largest branch of brachial plexus; motor to triceps, wrist extensors, finger extensors; sensory to posterior arm, posterior forearm, dorsal lateral hand
structures.location: Posterior cord C5-T1; winds around humerus in radial (spiral) groove with profunda brachii artery; pierces lateral intermuscular septum; divides at elbow into superficial and deep (posterior interosseous) branches
structures.clinicalNotes: Wrist drop: radial nerve injury in spiral groove (Saturday night palsy from humerus fracture). PIN palsy: posterior interosseous nerve compression in radial tunnel/supinator arcade of Frohse → finger drop without wrist drop. Anatomical snuffbox: branches at risk in distal radius fracture.

structures.name: Biceps Brachii
structures.function: Powerful supinator of forearm (most important function); flexes elbow; long head stabilises glenohumeral joint; the bicipital aponeurosis protects brachial artery and median nerve
structures.location: Two heads: short head from coracoid process, long head from supraglenoid tubercle via bicipital groove; inserts into radial tuberosity and bicipital aponeurosis
structures.bloodSupply: Brachial artery and anterior circumflex humeral artery
structures.clinicalNotes: Long head biceps tendinopathy: anterior shoulder pain, Speed's test positive. SLAP tear: long head anchor at glenoid. Distal biceps rupture: forearm supination weakness, Popeye deformity in arm. Biceps reflex tests C5-C6.

structures.name: Cephalic Vein
structures.function: Superficial venous drainage of the upper limb; travels in the deltopectoral groove; drains into axillary vein; commonly used for IV access and surgical cut-down
structures.location: Arises from dorsal venous arch; ascends lateral aspect of forearm; continues in lateral bicipital groove; runs in deltopectoral groove; pierces clavipectoral fascia to join axillary vein
structures.innervation: Lateral cutaneous nerve of forearm accompanies
structures.clinicalNotes: Preferred site for PICC line insertion and central venous catheter via cephalic cut-down. Cephalic vein used as arteriovenous fistula for haemodialysis. Anatomical variant: cephalic vein may terminate in external jugular, not axillary. Venepuncture at antecubital fossa uses median cubital vein (crosses from cephalic to basilic).

structures.name: Carpal Tunnel
structures.function: Fibro-osseous tunnel at wrist; transmits median nerve and 9 flexor tendons (FDS x4, FDP x4, FPL x1); floor: carpal bones; roof: flexor retinaculum (transverse carpal ligament)
structures.location: Between the pisiform/hamate on the ulnar side and scaphoid/trapezium on the radial side; covered by flexor retinaculum; ulnar nerve and artery pass through separate Guyon's canal
structures.bloodSupply: Radial and ulnar arteries via palmar arches
structures.clinicalNotes: Carpal tunnel syndrome: most common entrapment neuropathy. Risk factors: pregnancy, hypothyroidism, rheumatoid arthritis, diabetes, repetitive motion. Phalen's test (wrist flexion 60s) and Tinel's test (percussion). Treatment: splinting, steroid injection, surgical decompression (carpal tunnel release). Thenar wasting in chronic cases.

structures.name: Brachial Plexus
structures.function: Network of nerve roots C5-T1 supplying entire upper limb; divided into roots, trunks (upper/middle/lower), divisions (anterior/posterior), cords (lateral/medial/posterior), branches
structures.location: Emerges between scalenus anterior and medius; crosses posterior triangle of neck; passes under clavicle; enters axilla; cords surround axillary artery (named by their relation to artery)
structures.clinicalNotes: Erb's palsy (C5-C6): waiter's tip position from birth traction or shoulder dystocia. Klumpke's palsy (C8-T1): claw hand + Horner syndrome from inferior traction. Pancoast tumour (apex lung) → lower trunk compression. Thoracic outlet syndrome: compression between clavicle and first rib.

structures.name: Rotator Cuff
structures.function: Four muscles (SITS) stabilise glenohumeral joint by compressing humeral head into glenoid; supraspinatus initiates abduction; infraspinatus and teres minor externally rotate; subscapularis internally rotates
structures.location: SITS: Supraspinatus (supraspinous fossa → greater tuberosity superior facet), Infraspinatus (infraspinous fossa → middle facet), Teres minor (lateral scapular border → inferior facet), Subscapularis (subscapular fossa → lesser tuberosity)
structures.bloodSupply: Suprascapular artery, posterior circumflex humeral, subscapular artery
structures.innervation: Suprascapular nerve (C4-C6): supraspinatus + infraspinatus. Lower subscapular nerve: teres minor. Upper+lower subscapular: subscapularis
structures.clinicalNotes: Supraspinatus most commonly torn (impingement under acromion); painful arc 60-120° abduction. Full thickness tear: cannot initiate abduction (empty-can test). Repair by arthroscopic or open surgery with anchor sutures. MRI investigation of choice. Age-related degenerative tears commonest in 5th decade.
